papers.title_on_page: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers

claims.claim: Linearised self-attention is formally equivalent to early-1990s fast weight controllers, and linear attention has a memory capacity limit due to purely additive outer-product updates.
claims.scale: Theory plus synthetic retrieval, machine translation and language modelling experiments. Abstract confirms equivalence phrase and 'a memory capacity limitation of recent linearised softmax attention variants'.
claims.note: The 'purely additive outer-product updates' causal attribution is a mild paraphrase; the abstract describes replacing additive outer products with a delta-rule-like programming instruction.

claims.claim: Delta-rule update improves over the sum-update linear transformer on WikiText-103 at small scale.
claims.scale: Small (D=128, L=256, ~40M params) and medium (D=256, L=384, ~90M params). Table 2 test PPL: sum 38.3 vs delta 35.5 (small); sum 33.0 vs delta 31.5 (medium). Valid: 37.1 vs 34.1 and 31.1 vs 29.7. Standard softmax Transformer baseline is 34.1 (small) and 29.6 (medium) test, so delta still trails softmax at medium. Quote confirmed verbatim in HTML version.

The entry's remark about a '5-30M-adjacent' regime is irrelevant: smallest reported scale is 340M, not 5-30M. The abstract itself says 'LLaMA-architecture Transformer' rather than 'Transformer++'.
claims.note: Numbers verified from HTML Table 2; only first 100K of 117K chars read.

The abstract does not name cross-layer sharing; that parenthetical comes from the full paper. The role label 'origin of the idea' is questionable since Universal Transformers (2018) predates ALBERT.

papers.title_on_page: MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases
papers.role: most informative small-scale empirical comparison (immediate block-wise weight sharing in a decoder LM)

claims.claim: Proposes immediate block-wise weight sharing, which adds no model size and only a small latency cost.
claims.scale: sub-billion decoder LMs (125M/350M)
claims.note: Abstract confirms block-wise weight sharing with no model size increase and slight latency overhead. The fetch tool gave a paraphrase, so the exact word 'immediate' was not seen in the returned text.

claims.claim: The weight-sharing variant (MobileLLM-LS) gives a further accuracy gain over MobileLLM at small scales (0.7%/0.8% at 125M/350M).
claims.scale: 125M and 350M parameters
claims.note: Abstract mentions a further small accuracy improvement for MobileLLM-LS. The fetch summary did not return the specific 0.7%/0.8% figures, so those numbers were not independently confirmed here, though they match the published abstract as I recall it. Re-check against the abstract.

papers.title_on_page: Lessons on Parameter Sharing across Layers in Transformers
papers.role: alternative to full cross-layer sharing (sharing strategies for Transformers)

claims.claim: Proposes a parameter sharing method for Transformers that relaxes sharing one layer's parameters across all layers, reporting efficiency in parameter size and computation time.
claims.scale: Not stated in abstract; experiments are in machine translation (including large WMT datasets). Abstract does not compare directly to a standard Transformer.
claims.note: Confirmed. Three strategies named: Sequence, Cycle, Cycle (rev). The page is v4 (revised June 2023), first submitted April 2021. The quote 'We propose a parameter sharing method for Transformers' was not seen verbatim in the returned text.

papers.title_on_page: Universal Transformers
papers.role: origin of the idea (recurrence over depth with shared parameters)

claims.claim: Proposes the Universal Transformer, a parallel-in-time self-attentive recurrent sequence model. The abstract does not explicitly mention shared parameters across depth.
claims.scale: architectural/theoretical; reports gains on algorithmic tasks, LAMBADA, and WMT14 En-De (+0.9 BLEU); no model size stated in abstract.
claims.note: Confirmed as a self-attentive recurrent model generalizing the Transformer, with per-position dynamic halting. The abstract does not state weight sharing across depth, so the 'shared parameters' framing in the role field needs the full paper.

topics.topic: Mixture-of-Experts FFNs vs dense FFNs, especially at small scale

papers.title_on_page: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer

claims.claim: Introduces a sparsely-gated MoE layer of up to thousands of feed-forward experts, with conditional computation giving large capacity gains at small compute cost.
claims.scale: Up to 137B parameters in LSTM-based models (MoE applied between stacked LSTM layers); language modeling and machine translation; not small-scale Transformers
claims.note: Quote and 137B figure confirmed in abstract.

papers.title_on_page: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity

claims.claim: Top-1 routing (Switch) simplifies MoE and gives pre-training speedups over dense T5 baselines at matched compute.
claims.scale: T5-Base/Large based models up to trillion-parameter sparse models (4x speedup over T5-XXL); not small-scale (<=350M) in headline results
claims.note: Abstract says 'up to 7x increases in pre-training speed' with same computational resources. The abstract does not explicitly say 'top-1'; that detail is from the paper body (simplified routing). Speedup is in steps/time-to-quality, not small-scale.

papers.title_on_page: Scaling Laws for Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts

claims.claim: Introduces expert granularity as a hyperparameter; the efficiency gap between dense and MoE models widens with scale.
claims.scale: Scaling-law fits over model size, training tokens and granularity; smallest sizes not verified from the abstract
claims.note: Phrase confirmed in abstract. Abstract-only check; exact size range not verified.

claims.claim: Setting expert size equal to the feed-forward layer size is suboptimal at almost any compute budget.
claims.scale: Scaling-law fits across compute budgets; empirical fit extrapolated, not small-scale specific
claims.note: Phrase confirmed in abstract.

papers.title_on_page: OLMoE: Open Mixture-of-Experts Language Models

claims.claim: A fully open sparse MoE LM with 7B total parameters using about 1B active per token.
claims.scale: 1B active / 7B total parameters, pretrained on 5T tokens; not small-scale, but fully open weights, data, code and logs
claims.note: Quote verbatim in abstract. Abstract also mentions MoE training experiments and routing analysis.

papers.title_on_page: Sparse Upcycling: Training Mixture-of-Experts from Dense Checkpoints

claims.claim: Initializes a sparse MoE from a dense checkpoint, reusing sunk dense training cost; upcycled models outperform dense counterparts with about 50% of the dense pretraining cost.
claims.scale: T5 Base, Large, XL language models and ViT Base and Large vision models; evaluated on SuperGLUE and ImageNet; not small-scale (<=350M) beyond T5-Base/ViT-Base
claims.note: Quote confirmed in abstract. The scale note in the proposal ('large-scale') is slightly loose; models are Base to XL. The 50% figure is the extra compute relative to initial dense pretraining cost.

topics.topic: Position encoding in causal LMs: RoPE vs ALiBi vs no positional encoding (NoPE)

papers.title_on_page: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding

claims.claim: Introduces RoPE, encoding absolute position with a rotation matrix while incorporating explicit relative-position dependency into self-attention.
claims.scale: Abstract gives no model size; evaluated on long text classification benchmarks (sizes not checked in full paper).
claims.note: Both quoted phrases appear in the abstract.

claims.claim: RoPE gives decaying inter-token dependency with relative distance and is compatible with linear self-attention.
claims.scale: Property claimed in the abstract; no model size or small-scale ablation stated on the abstract page.
claims.note: Abstract lists decay with distance and the ability to equip linear self-attention with relative position encoding. The quoted phrase attached to this claim only covers the relative-dependency part.

papers.title_on_page: Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation

claims.claim: ALiBi biases query-key attention scores with a distance-proportional penalty, enabling extrapolation to longer inputs than trained on.
claims.scale: 1.3B parameters, trained on length 1024, extrapolating to length 2048 (confirmed on abstract page).
claims.note: Quote verified.

claims.claim: ALiBi matches a sinusoidal-embedding model trained on length 2048 while training faster and using less memory.
claims.scale: 1.3B parameters (confirmed). The 11% faster and 11% less memory figures are verified.
claims.note: The dataset attribution is wrong. The abstract page does not say what the 1.3B model was trained on. WikiText-103 appears separately as a benchmark where ALiBi outperforms other position methods. Remove 'WikiText-103' from this claim's scale note unless the full paper confirms it.

papers.title_on_page: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information

claims.claim: Causal LMs with no explicit positional encoding (NoPE) remain competitive with standard Transformers.
claims.scale: Abstract says the result holds across different datasets, model sizes and sequence lengths. It lists no parameter counts.
claims.note: Quote verified. The paper does not use the term NoPE; it says models without positional encodings.

claims.claim: Models without positional encoding acquire an implicit notion of absolute position through the network, which probing reveals.
claims.scale: Probing experiments; sizes not stated on the abstract page.
claims.note: Quote verified. The paper attributes this to the causal attention mask.

papers.title_on_page: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers

claims.claim: NoPE outperforms explicit positional encodings (ALiBi, RoPE, APE) for downstream length generalization at no extra computation cost.
claims.scale: Decoder-only Transformers; model sizes not stated on the abstract page. The tasks are reasoning and math.
claims.note: Quote verified. The abstract compares five methods: APE, T5's Relative PE, ALiBi, Rotary and NoPE. The claim leaves out T5 Relative PE, so 'outperforms other explicit methods' covers more than the three listed.

claims.claim: ALiBi, Rotary and APE are not well suited for length generalization in downstream tasks.
claims.scale: Decoder-only Transformers; sizes not stated on the abstract page. Results are on downstream reasoning and math tasks.
claims.note: Quote verified.

topics.topic: Normalization and FFN activation in decoders: pre-LN vs post-LN, RMSNorm, SwiGLU/GLU variants, QK-norm and logit stability

papers.title_on_page: On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture

claims.claim: Post-LN Transformers have large expected gradients near the output layer at initialization, which motivates warm-up; Pre-LN placement removes the need for warm-up.
claims.scale: Theoretical analysis plus machine translation experiments (ICML 2020); model sizes not verified from the abstract.
claims.note: Abstract summary matches. The quoted wording was not confirmed verbatim, because the fetch tool paraphrased the abstract. Treat the quote as approximate.

papers.title_on_page: Root Mean Square Layer Normalization

claims.claim: RMSNorm drops mean-centering from LayerNorm, is cheaper, and matches LayerNorm performance.
claims.scale: Several tasks and architectures; sizes not stated in the abstract. The 7%~64% running-time reduction is as reported.
claims.note: The 7%~64% quote was confirmed. 'Matches' should be softened to 'comparable', which is the abstract's wording. The paper also introduces pRMSNorm.

papers.title_on_page: GLU Variants Improve Transformer

claims.claim: GLU-family feed-forward activations (e.g. SwiGLU, GEGLU) improve over ReLU and GELU FFNs in Transformers.
claims.scale: Transformer FFN sublayers; model sizes not stated in the abstract.
claims.note: The abstract says only that 'some' variants beat ReLU and GELU. The fetched abstract summary does not name SwiGLU or GEGLU, so those names come from the paper body, which was not checked. The quote could not be checked verbatim.

papers.title_on_page: Query-Key Normalization for Transformers

claims.claim: QKNorm normalizes queries and keys before the attention dot product, improving low-resource translation.
claims.scale: Low-resource bilingual translation: five TED Talks and IWSLT'15 pairs; average gain 0.928 BLEU over prior bilingual benchmarks. Model sizes not verified.
claims.note: QKNorm applies L2 normalization to queries and keys along the head dimension, then scales by a learnable parameter instead of 1/sqrt(d). The 0.928 BLEU figure was confirmed. This is a small-scale translation result and does not show decoder LM logit stability.

papers.title_on_page: Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities

claims.claim: Training instabilities that appear only at large scale also appear in small models trained at high learning rates, so small proxies can be used to study them.
claims.scale: Small models; exact parameter counts not verified from the abstract.
claims.note: The quote was confirmed. The instabilities studied are growing attention logits and output logits diverging from log probabilities. Mitigations from large scale work similarly at small scale. The paper also covers warm-up, weight decay and muParam.

papers.title_on_page: Scaling Vision Transformers to 22 Billion Parameters

claims.claim: A recipe for stable training of a 22B-parameter ViT is presented. The abstract does not name QK-normalization; that detail must be checked in the paper body before citing it for QK-norm.
claims.scale: 22B parameters, vision (ViT-22B), not a decoder LM.
claims.note: The abstract summary supports the training-recipe claim. It does not mention QK-normalization, so the QK-norm detail remains unverified here and must be checked in the paper body. The quote could not be confirmed verbatim.

topics.topic: Tied input/output embeddings, especially for small models

papers.title_on_page: Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models
papers.role: origin of the commitment (introduces tying input and output embeddings; EACL 2017)

claims.claim: Recommends tying input and output embeddings; the output matrix works as a valid word embedding.
claims.scale: neural language models; qualitative, no sizes in abstract
claims.note: Abstract also says tying significantly reduces perplexity across several models. Verified via summary; verbatim quote not confirmed by fetch tool.

claims.claim: Weight tying can shrink translation models to less than half original size without harming performance.
claims.scale: neural translation models; sizes not given in abstract
claims.note: Matches abstract (paraphrased by fetch tool); exact quote wording unverified.

papers.title_on_page: Tying Word Vectors and Word Classifiers: A Loss Framework for Language Modeling
papers.role: origin / alternative (independent proposal with loss-framework justification)

claims.claim: Tying input embedding and output projection greatly reduces trainable parameters; framework reaches state of the art on Penn Treebank with several network models.
claims.scale: RNN word LMs on PTB; no parameter counts or perplexities in abstract
claims.note: Abstract says 'greatly reducing the number of trainable variables'. Entry's quote wording about 'a variety of network models' not verbatim-confirmed. 'Sound approach' is the entry's gloss, not an abstract claim.

papers.title_on_page: MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases
papers.role: empirical comparison at small scale (embedding sharing is one of several combined choices; effect not isolated)

claims.claim: Deep-and-thin architecture with embedding sharing and GQA beats prior SOTA by 2.7%/4.3% accuracy at 125M/350M.
claims.scale: 125M and 350M params; gain is for combined architecture, not embedding sharing alone
claims.note: Numbers match. Abstract also reports MobileLLM-LS (block-wise weight sharing) adds 0.7%/0.8%. Sub-billion models, above 5-30M target range.

papers.title_on_page: SmolLM2: When Smol Goes Big -- Data-Centric Training of a Small Language Model
papers.role: context only (small-model recipe; abstract does not discuss tied embeddings)

claims.claim: 1.7B small LM trained on ~11T tokens that outperforms Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama3.2-1B; no tied-embedding claim in abstract.
claims.scale: 1.7B params; far above 5-30M target range; not evidence on tying
claims.note: Abstract confirms 1.7B, ~11T tokens, outperforming Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama3.2-1B. Confirmed absence of tying discussion in abstract.

topics.topic: Small-scale LM architecture findings: TinyStories depth/width, deep-and-thin vs wide at small scale, model shape in scaling laws

papers.title_on_page: TinyStories: How Small Can Language Models Be and Still Speak Coherent English?

claims.claim: A TinyStories-style synthetic children's-story corpus lets much smaller LMs produce coherent English than standard models.
claims.scale: Abstract: models below 10M total parameters, versus ~125M baselines (GPT-Neo small, GPT-2 small); also mentions single-transformer-block models.
claims.note: Quote confirmed in abstract. Dataset is GPT-3.5/GPT-4-generated stories using vocabulary of a 3-4 year old.

papers.title_on_page: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

claims.claim: Within a wide range, network width or depth has minimal effect on loss compared with total parameter count, compute and data.
claims.scale: Abstract gives no numeric range for the width/depth claim; the 1e3 to 1e9 parameter span is not stated on the abstract page and was not verified here.
claims.note: Quote confirmed. The proposed scale note is unverified from the abstract and should be checked in the paper body. Also, the result is for a fixed non-embedding parameter count, so it does not speak to extremely deep-thin or wide-shallow shapes.

papers.title_on_page: MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases

claims.claim: At sub-billion scale, deep-and-thin architectures with embedding sharing and grouped-query attention are the chosen design, rather than wide-and-shallow.
claims.scale: Abstract names 125M and 350M parameter MobileLLM models (sub-billion).
claims.note: Quote confirmed. The abstract argues architecture matters more than data or parameter count at this scale. It also introduces MobileLLM-LS with block-wise weight sharing. The 'rather than wide-and-shallow' comparison is implied by the abstract; the supporting ablations are in the paper body and were not checked.

papers.title_on_page: The Impact of Depth on Compositional Generalization in Transformer Language Models

claims.claim: At constant total parameter count, deeper Transformers generalize more compositionally than shallower ones, trading depth for width.
claims.scale: 41M, 134M and 374M parameters, total parameters held constant across depth configurations.
claims.note: Quote confirmed. The abstract caveat is that the benefit of extra layers diminishes rapidly. The claim concerns compositional generalization, not language-modeling loss or perplexity, which the abstract says is a separate matter.

topics.topic: Architecture screening with synthetic tasks: MQAR/associative recall, MAD, and limits of synthetic proxies

papers.title_on_page: Zoology: Measuring and Improving Recall in Efficient Language Models

claims.claim: 70M attention model beats 1.4B gated-convolution model on associative recall.
claims.scale: 70M vs 1.4B; I recall this headline comparison from the paper's intro rather than the abstract. The fetched abstract summary only mentions parameter-efficiency differences, and the 17 models trained were on the Pile.
claims.note: Verbatim quote not confirmed against the abstract text (fetch gave a paraphrase). Cite the intro or figure, not the abstract.

claims.claim: Paper reformalizes associative recall as MQAR to match real language better; attention outperforms gated convolutions by a large margin on it.
claims.scale: Synthetic task; the abstract reports 17 attention and gated-convolution LMs, a gap of up to 2.1 ppl on the Pile, ~82% of the gap attributed to associative recall, and hybrids closing 97.4% of the gap.
claims.note: MQAR introduction is confirmed. 'Large margin' is consistent with the paper but the abstract summary did not state it explicitly.

papers.title_on_page: Mechanistic Design and Scaling of Hybrid Architectures

claims.claim: Curated synthetic tasks are predictive of scaling behavior of architectures.
claims.scale: Over 500 LMs, 70M-7B parameters, compute-optimal and state-optimal scaling analyses. Exceeds the 350M small-scale band.
claims.note: Abstract confirms synthetic-task performance correlates with compute-optimal perplexity. Wording about 'scaling laws' is from memory of the abstract. Correlation is with compute-optimal perplexity, not a guarantee of ranking everywhere.

claims.claim: MAD synthetics correlate with compute-optimal perplexity.
claims.scale: 70M-7B parameters, over 500 models.
claims.note: Confirmed by the abstract summary. Note the abstract frames this as a proxy for evaluating new architectures, and reports outperforming Transformer++, Hyena and Mamba.

papers.title_on_page: In-context Learning and Induction Heads

claims.claim: Induction heads are proposed as the mechanism for most in-context learning, motivating copy/recall probes.
claims.scale: Abstract: strong causal evidence for small attention-only models, correlational evidence for larger models with MLPs. No parameter counts stated. Scale unverified.
claims.note: The 'might constitute the mechanism' hedge is the abstract's own. The 'why copy/recall tasks are used as probes' part is the table author's inference, not a claim in the abstract.

papers.title_on_page: Hungry Hungry Hippos: Towards Language Modeling with State Space Models

claims.claim: H3 matches attention on synthetic languages testing recall of earlier tokens, establishing synthetics as an early architecture screen.
claims.scale: Synthetic tasks, no parameter count in the abstract.
claims.note: The 'matches attention on synthetic languages' part is confirmed. 'Establishing synthetics as an early screen' is overreach. The paper only motivates H3 from synthetic failures of prior SSMs.

claims.claim: A 125M-parameter H3-attention hybrid outperforms Transformers on OpenWebText by 1.0 PPL.
claims.scale: 125M parameters, within the 350M band. Pure H3 comes close to Transformers on OpenWebText. Hybrids were scaled to 2.7B for Pile results.
claims.note: The fetched abstract summary did not repeat the 125M / 1.0 PPL numbers. They match my recollection of the abstract, but verify the exact numbers against the abstract or Table before final citation.

topics.topic: Origins of the baseline decoder: Transformer, GPT-style causal decoding, LLaMA recipe (pre-RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE)

papers.title_on_page: Attention Is All You Need

claims.claim: Introduces the Transformer, built solely from attention with no recurrence or convolution.
claims.scale: WMT14 En-De (28.4 BLEU) and En-Fr (41.8 BLEU, 3.5 days on 8 GPUs). The ~65M base-model size is from the paper body and was not re-checked here.
claims.note: The fetched abstract confirms the attention-only architecture. The fetch tool truncated the quote, but the 'dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely' wording matches the known abstract. The original is an encoder-decoder, so it is not itself a decoder-only baseline.

papers.title_on_page: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2); not on arXiv, only mirrors and secondary sources found

claims.claim: Establishes GPT-style left-to-right causal decoder-only LM as the baseline decoder form.
claims.scale: Secondary sources describe a 1.5B-parameter largest model trained on WebText. The 124M-1.5B family range was not confirmed from a primary source.
claims.note: No primary text was fetched and the quote is marked unverified, so do not cite verbatim. Authorship (Radford et al., Feb 2019, OpenAI) is confirmed by search. A PDF mirror exists, for example gwern.net/docs/ai/gpt/2019-radford.pdf. The causal decoder-only framing is also arguably credited to GPT-1 (Radford 2018) and Liu et al. 2018.

papers.title_on_page: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
papers.role: origin of the commitment (recipe: pre-RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE)

claims.claim: Llama-style recipe trained only on public data reaches strong performance.
claims.scale: 7B to 65B parameters, trillions of tokens. LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks. Not evaluated at 5-30M.
claims.note: The abstract supports the public-data and performance claim. The fetched abstract summary does not mention pre-norm, SwiGLU or RoPE. Those details come from the paper body and were not checked here.

papers.title_on_page: Root Mean Square Layer Normalization

claims.claim: RMSNorm drops mean-centering and matches LayerNorm quality while running faster.
claims.scale: Running-time reduction of 7%-64% across several models, per the abstract. Exact model sizes were not checked.
claims.note: The abstract supports the 7%-64% figure and the comparable-performance claim. It hypothesizes that re-centering invariance is dispensable.

papers.title_on_page: On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture

claims.claim: Pre-LN lets Transformers train without a learning-rate warm-up, which motivates the pre-norm default in Llama-style decoders.
claims.scale: Machine translation, and I recall BERT pretraining as well. Model sizes were not verified. The paper is not about decoder-only LMs.
claims.note: The first half is supported: the abstract says Pre-LN has well-behaved gradients at init and motivates removing warm-up, with comparable results and less tuning. The clause about the Llama default is the citer's inference, not a claim made in the paper.

papers.title_on_page: GLU Variants Improve Transformer

claims.claim: GLU FFN variants, including SwiGLU, improve quality over ReLU or GELU FFN.
claims.scale: Transformer sequence-to-sequence feed-forward sublayers. Exact sizes were not verified; the paper body is T5-style pretraining and fine-tuning.
claims.note: The abstract says only that 'some' variants yield quality improvements. It does not name SwiGLU, which is in the paper body. Wording should say 'some variants'.

papers.title_on_page: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding

claims.claim: RoPE encodes position by rotating query and key vectors and gives flexible sequence length.
claims.scale: RoFormer is evaluated on long-text classification benchmarks and pretraining. Exact sizes were not verified.
claims.note: The abstract says RoPE encodes absolute position with a rotation matrix and builds relative dependency into self-attention. It lists flexible sequence length, decaying dependency with distance, and linear-attention compatibility. The 'rotating query and key' detail is from the body, not the abstract.
